newsitem.title: GERMANY: German women take over for carnival.
newsitem.headline: German women take over for carnival.

text.p: Hundreds of women dressed as soldiers, witches and devils stormed Bonn's town hall on Thursday and demanded the mayor's key to mark the German carnival day when women take over.
"Women take charge today and get their own back on men." said Gudrun Zeitz, a government secretary whose face was painted with a clown's smile. "Soon it will be this way always."
The Rhineland region's "Weiberfastnacht" or "Wenches' Feasting Day" is the first of a series of so-called "crazy days" when Germans drop their reserve, don fancy-dress and accost strangers.

Thousands of merry-makers dressed as clowns, angels and aliens thronged Bonn's Beuel district to watch the women take over the town hall as people on hundreds of floats showered sweets and flowers into the crowds.
"It's really great that once a year Germans can stop being so serious and enjoy themselves," said Rosa Abarco Toro, a Peruvian studying in Germany.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl agreed. "Carnival signals that we are here and that we love life," he said after meeting carnival princes and princesses.
Carnival in Germany has its roots in pagan ceremonies to chase away the evil spirits of winter.

Under Christianity, the festivities became linked with a last burst of merriment before the Lent fasting period begins 40 days before Easter. It is the same celebration as Brazil's Carnivale and the New Orleans Mardis Gras.
But women felt that men dominated the proceedings, which are run by local carnival clubs headed largely by men who dress up in elaborate mock soldier unifoms.
In 1824 the washerwomen of Beuel, then a poor village near Bonn, decided that women should have a day of their own and should storm the town hall, led by the year's "washing princess."
Nowadays women all over the Rhine region take to the streets for a night out without men. They are also allowed to slice off the tie of any man they see wearing one.
"But the men don't stay at home. They come out as well to hunt the wild women," said Magdelena Marcus, a secretary. "If we catch a man then he will have to pay for our drinks."
The Rhineland carnival comes to a climax next Monday with the huge Rosenmontagzug (Rose Monday Parade) in Cologne, a procession featuring over 7,000 people and 300 horses.
